verses.zh: 国为列国之首，人最着名，且为以色列家所归向，在锡安和撒马利亚山安逸无虑的，有祸了！
verses.en: Woe[NOTE:1] to those who live in ease in Zion,[NOTE:2] to those who feel secure on Mount Samaria.They think of themselves as[NOTE:3] the elite class of the best nation.The family[NOTE:4] of Israel looks to them for leadership.[NOTE:5]
notes: On the Hebrew term הוֹי (hoy; “ah, woe”) as a term of mourning, see the notes in 5:16, 18.
Zion is a reference to Jerusalem.

The words “They think of themselves as” are supplied in the translation for clarification. In the Hebrew text the term נְקֻבֵי (nequvey; “distinguished ones, elite”) is in apposition to the substantival participles in the first line.
Heb “house.”
Heb “comes to them.”

verses.zh: 你们要过到甲尼察看，从那里往大城哈马去，又下到非利士人的迦特。看那些比你们的国还强吗？境界比你们的境界还宽吗？
verses.en: They say to the people:[NOTE:1] “Journey over to Calneh and look at it;then go from there to Hamath-Rabbah;[NOTE:2] then go down to Gath of the Philistines.Are they superior to our two[NOTE:3] kingdoms?Is their territory larger than yours?”[NOTE:4]
notes: The words “They say to the people” are interpretive and supplied in the translation for clarification. The translation understands v. 2 as the boastful words, which the leaders (described in v. 1) spoke to those who came to them (v. 1b). Some interpret v. 2 differently, understanding the words as directed to the leaders by the prophet. Verse 2b would then be translated: “Are you (i.e., Israel and Judah) better than these kingdoms (i.e., Calneh, etc.)? Is your border larger than their border?” (This reading requires an emendation of the Hebrew text toward the end of the verse.) In this case the verse is a reminder to Judah/Israel that they are not superior to other nations, which have already fallen victim to military conquest. Consequently Judah/Israel should not expect to escape the same fate. Following this line of interpretation, some take v. 2 as a later addition since the Assyrians under Tiglath-Pileser III conquered Calneh, Hamath, and Gath after the time of Amos’ ministry. However, this conclusion is not necessary since the kingdoms mentioned here had suffered military setbacks prior to Amos’ time as well. See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 201-4.
Or “Great Hamath” (cf. NIV); or “Hamath the great” (cf. KJV, NAB, NASB, NRSV); the word “rabbah” means “great” in Hebrew.
Heb “to these,” referring to Judah and Israel (see v. 1a).

Both rhetorical questions in this verse expect the answer “no.” If these words do come from the leaders, then this verse underscores their self-delusion of power (compare 6:13). The prophet had no such mistaken sense of national grandeur (7:2, 5).

verses.zh: 你们以为降祸的日子还远，坐在位上尽行强暴（或译：行强暴使审判临近）。
verses.en: You refuse to believe a day of disaster will come,[NOTE:1] but you establish a reign of violence.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “those who push away a day of disaster.”

Heb “you bring near a seat of violence.” The precise meaning of the Hebrew term שֶׁבֶת (shevet, “seat, sitting”) is unclear in this context. The translation assumes that it refers to a throne from which violence (in the person of the oppressive leaders) reigns. Another option is that the expression refers not to the leaders’ oppressive rule, but to the coming judgment when violence will overtake the nation in the person of enemy invaders.

verses.zh: 你们躺卧在象牙床上，舒身在榻上，吃群中的羊羔，棚里的牛犊；
verses.en: They lie around on beds decorated with ivory[NOTE:1] and sprawl out on their couches.They eat lambs from the flockand calves from the middle of the pen.
notes: Heb “beds of ivory.”

verses.zh: 弹琴鼓瑟，唱消闲的歌曲，为自己制造乐器，如同大卫所造的；
verses.en: They sing[NOTE:1] to the tune of[NOTE:2] stringed instruments;[NOTE:3] like David they invent[NOTE:4] musical instruments.
notes: The meaning of the Hebrew verb פָּרַט (parat), which occurs only here in the OT, is unclear. Some translate “strum,” “pluck,” or “improvise.”
Heb “upon the mouth of,” that is, “according to.”
The stringed instruments mentioned here are probably harps (cf. NIV, NRSV) or lutes (cf. NEB).

The meaning of the Hebrew phrase חָשְׁבוּ לָהֶם (khashevu lahem) is uncertain. Various options include: (1) “they think their musical instruments are like David’s”; (2) “they consider themselves musicians like David”; (3) “they esteem musical instruments highly like David”; (4) “they improvise [new songs] for themselves [on] instruments like David”; and (5) “they invent musical instruments like David.” However, the most commonly accepted interpretation is that given in the translation (see S. M. Paul, Amos [Hermeneia], 206-7).

verses.zh: 以大碗喝酒，用上等的油抹身，却不为约瑟的苦难担忧。
verses.en: They drink wine from sacrificial bowls[NOTE:1] and pour the very best oils on themselves.[NOTE:2] Yet they are not concerned over[NOTE:3] the ruin[NOTE:4] of Joseph.
notes: Perhaps some religious rite is in view, or the size of the bowls is emphasized (i.e., bowls as large as sacrificial bowls).
Heb “with the best of oils they anoint [themselves].”
Or “not sickened by.”
The ruin of Joseph may refer to the societal disintegration in Israel, or to the effects of the impending judgment.

verses.zh: 所以这些人必在被掳的人中首先被掳，舒身的人荒宴之乐必消灭了。
verses.en: Therefore they will now be the first to go into exile,[NOTE:1] and the religious banquets[NOTE:2] where they sprawl on couches[NOTE:3] will end.
notes: Heb “they will go into exile at the head of the exiles.”

Religious banquets. This refers to the מַרְזֵחַ (marzeakh), a type of pagan religious banquet popular among the upper class of Israel at this time and apparently associated with mourning. See P. King, Amos, Hosea, Micah, 137-61; J. L. McLaughlin, The “Marzeah” in the Prophetic Literature (VTSup). Scholars debate whether at this banquet the dead were simply remembered or actually venerated in a formal, cultic sense.
Heb “of the sprawled out.” See v. 4.

verses.zh: 主耶和华万军之　神指着自己起誓说，我憎恶雅各的荣华，厌弃他的宫殿；因此我必将城和其中所有的都交付敌人。
verses.en: The Sovereign Lord confirms this oath by his very own life.[NOTE:1] The Lord God of Heaven’s Armies is speaking:“I despise Jacob’s arrogance;I hate their[NOTE:2] fortresses.I will hand over to their enemies[NOTE:3] the city of Samaria[NOTE:4] and everything in it.”
notes: Heb “swears by his life”; or “swears by himself.”
Heb “his,” referring to Jacob, which stands here for the nation of Israel.
The words “to their enemies” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “the city”; this probably refers to the city of Samaria (cf. 6:1), which in turn, by metonymy, represents the entire northern kingdom.

verses.zh: 那时，若在一房之内剩下十个人，也都必死。
verses.en: If 10 men are left in one house, they too will die.

verses.zh: 死人的伯叔，就是烧他尸首的，要将这尸首搬到房外，问房屋内间的人说：「你那里还有人没有？」他必说：「没有」；又说：「不要作声，因为我们不可提耶和华的名。」
verses.en: When their close relatives, the ones who will burn the corpses,[NOTE:1] pick up their bodies to remove the bones from the house, they will say to anyone who is in the inner rooms of the house, “Is anyone else with you?” He will respond, “No one.” Then he will say, “Hush! Don’t invoke the Lord’s name!”[NOTE:2]
notes: The translation assumes that “their relatives” and “the ones who will burn the corpses” are in apposition. Another option is to take them as distinct individuals, in which case one could translate, “When their close relatives and the ones who will burn the corpses pick up…” The meaning of the form translated “the ones who burn the corpses” is uncertain. Another option is to translate, “the ones who prepare the corpses for burial” (cf. NASB “undertaker”; cf. also CEV). See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 215-16.

This verse is notoriously difficult to interpret. The Hebrew text literally reads, “And he will lift him up, his uncle, and the one burning him, to bring out bones from the house. And he will say to the one who is in the inner parts of the house, ‘Is there [anyone] still with you?’ And he will say, ‘No one.’ And he will say, ‘Hush, for not to invoke the name of the Lord.’” The translation assumes that the singular pronominal and verbal forms throughout the verse are collective or distributive. This last sentence has been interpreted in several ways: a command not to call on the name of the Lord out of fear that he might return again in judgment; the realization that it is not appropriate to seek a blessing in the Lord’s name upon the dead in the house since the judgment was deserved; an angry refusal to call on the Lord out of a sense that he has betrayed his people in allowing them to suffer.

verses.zh: 看哪，耶和华出令，大房就被攻破，小屋就被打裂。
verses.en: Indeed, look! The Lord is giving the command.[NOTE:1] He will smash the large house to bitsand the small house into little pieces.
notes: Or “is issuing the decree.”

verses.zh: 马岂能在崖石上奔跑？人岂能在那里用牛耕种呢？你们却使公平变为苦胆，使公义的果子变为茵蔯。
verses.en: Can horses run on rocky cliffs?Can one plow the sea with oxen?[NOTE:1] Yet you have turned justice into a poisonous plantand the fruit of righteous actions into a bitter plant.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Does one plow with oxen?” This obviously does not fit the parallelism, for the preceding rhetorical question requires the answer, “Of course not!” An error of fusion has occurred in the Hebrew, with the word יָם (yam, “sea”) being accidentally added as a plural ending to the collective noun בָּקָר (baqar, “oxen”). A proper division of the consonants produces the above translation, which fits the parallelism and also anticipates the answer, “Of course not!”

The botanical imagery, when juxtaposed with the preceding rhetorical questions, vividly depicts and emphasizes how the Israelites have perverted justice and violated the created order by their morally irrational behavior.

verses.zh: 你们喜爱虚浮的事，自夸说，我们不是凭自己的力量取了角吗？
verses.en: You are happy because you conquered Lo Debar.[NOTE:1] You say, “Did we not conquer Karnaim[NOTE:2] by our own power?”
notes: Heb “those who rejoice over Lo Debar.”sn Lo Debar was located across the Jordan River in Gilead, which the Israelite army had conquered. However, there is stinging irony here, for in Hebrew the name Lo-Debar means “nothing.” In reality Israel was happy over nothing of lasting consequence.

Karnaim was also located across the Jordan River. The name in Hebrew means “double horned.” Since an animal’s horn was a symbol of strength (see Deut 33:17), the Israelites boasted in this victory over a town whose very name symbolized military power.

verses.zh: 耶和华万军之　神说：以色列家啊，我必兴起一国攻击你们；他们必欺压你们，从哈马口直到亚拉巴的河。
verses.en: “Look! I am about to bring[NOTE:1] a nation against you, family[NOTE:2] of Israel,”the Lord, the God who commands armies, is speaking.“They will oppress[NOTE:3] you all the way from Lebo Hamath[NOTE:4] to the stream of the rift valley.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “raise up” (KJV, NASB); cf. NIV “stir up.”
Heb “house.”

Once again there is irony in the divine judgment. The oppressive nation itself will suffer oppression. The verb “oppress” (לָחַץ, lakhats) in this verse is not the same as that used in 4:1 (עָשַׁק, ʿashaq).

Or “the entrance to Hamath.” The Hebrew term לְבוֹא (levoʾ) can either be translated or considered a part of the place name. This may be a site some 44 miles north of Damascus (see T.R. Hobbs, 2 Kings [WBC], 182).

Lebo Hamath refers to the northern border of Israel, the stream of the rift valley to its southern border. See Num 34:8, 12; 1 Kgs 8:65; 2 Kgs 14:25. The southern border is named in various ways, as the Dead Sea, the stream of the rift valley (a stream which flows into the Dead Sea, possibly Zered at the south end), and the Brook of Egypt (the southwestern boundary). Through this invader the Lord would reverse the victories and territorial expansion Israel experienced during the reign of Jeroboam II.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 6:1-3

1Woe to those who are at ease in Zion

And to those who feel secure in the mountain of Samaria,

The distinguished men of the foremost of nations,

To whom the house of Israel comes.

2Go over to Calneh and look,

And go from there to Hamath the great,

Then go down to Gath of the Philistines.

Are they better than these kingdoms,

Or is their territory greater than yours?

3Do you put off the day of calamity,

And would you bring near the seat of violence?

6:1 "Woe" The pronunciation of His Hebrew word sounds like exasperated or sorrowful feelings. This term
(BDB 222) characterizes the book of Lamentations. The Prophets often used the literary form
(a 3-2 beat) of a funeral dirge to express the disapproval of God and His coming judgment. This term is recurrent
in Isaiah.

- negative in Isa. 1:4,24; 5:8,11,18,20,21,22; 10:1; 17:12; 18:1; 28:1; 29:1,15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1; 45:9,10

- neutral in Isa. 10:5

- positive in Isa. 55:1, and Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 22:13,18; 23:1; 30:7; 34:5; 47:6; 48:1; 50:27)

This INTERJECTION is followed by a series of PARTICIPLES, which
carries the "woe" thought with each of them (Amos 6:1-7).

▣ "to those who are at ease" There is no VERB. This phrase is used as a
SUBSTANTIVE. It has the prophetic connotation of "careless, wanton, arrogant" (BDB 983, KB 1375,
cf. Isa. 32:9,11; Zech. 1:15; and Ps. 123:4). It was not their leisure or wealth or social status that was the problem,
but their trust in these things instead of God.

The group is characterized in several ways in the next few verses:

- those who feel secure, Amos 6:1b

- you who put away the evil day, Amos 6:3

- those who lie on beds of ivory, Amos 6:4

- those who improvise (sing idle songs), Amos 6:5

- those who drink wine from sacrificial bowls, Amos 6:6

All of these phrases have the DEFINITE ARTICLE plus a PARTICIPLE.

▣ "in Zion" This seems to be parallel to "in the mountain of Samaria" (the capital of the Northern
Ten Tribes). However, Zion is one of the seven hills of Jerusalem. Therefore, this could mean

- covenant people as a whole, Amos 3:1; 6:8

- Judah and Israel were both sinful and guilty

- a literary parallel, but with no distinction intended

- The Jewish Publication Society of America (JPSOA, p. 1187 footnote d) suggests a possible emendation, "to Zion,"
which is "Joseph," which would parallel "hill of Samaria" better. Joseph is referred to in Amos 6:6, and in Amos 5:6,15
it was a way to refer to the northern tribes.

- Both the Peshitta and LXX translate it as referring to Israel's opposition to Judah.

- LXX ‒ "set at naught Zion"

- Peshitta ‒ "despise Zion"

- former leaders from the surrounding nations, with whom Israel was trying to make security agreements to protect
themselves from the judgment of YHWH (i.e. Assyrian exile)

The MT has the VERB "come" (BDB 97, KB 112, Qal PERFECT with

followed by NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB.

6:2 Depending on how one interprets Amos 6:1, this verse would be

- Amos' words to the arrogant leadership of the covenant people (Judah and Israel) similar to Amos 9:7. However,
this involved some textual emendations (cf. UBS, Handbook, #31, p. 289)

- the leaders' comments to the people (cf. NET Bible, Tyndale commentary)

▣ "Calneh" This was a fortified city in Syria (BDB 484, cf. Isa. 10:9), which was destroyed by
Tiglath-pileser III in 738 B.C. It became a proverb of the coming exile of Israel (cf. Isa. 10:9-11).
It was on this occasion that the king of Israel, Menahen, began to give tribute to Assyria.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA, #19

▣ "Hamath" The Anchor Bible Dictionary, vol. 3, p. 33, has a good brief comment.

"A city in Syria, the southern border of which often became part of the formula for
the northern idealized border of Israel (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:65; 1 Chr. 13:5). The city was an object of the
Assyrian conquest (Isa. 36:19), and some of its inhabitants were exiled and settled in Israel (2 Kgs. 17:24)."

It (BDB 333) was located about 150 miles north of the city of Dan on the Orantes River.

▣ "Gath" The Philistines established five city-states in southwest Judah on the coastal
plain. Four of those cities are mentioned earlier in Amos 1:6-8, Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, and Ekron). Gath (BDB 387 III)
was captured by David in 1 Chronicles 18 and is also mentioned in Micah 1:10. It was later destroyed by the Assyrians.

▣ "Or is their territory greater than yours?" The JPSOA suggests an emendation that reverses this
phrase, "Or is your territory larger than theirs," p. 1187 footnote, "f." The UBS Text Project, p. 287, suggests the translation,
"if small states like Kalneh, Hamath, Gath are flourishing, how much more this will be the case with the greater States of Judah
and Israel!" It also suggests an interpretation, "This discourse reflects the blind self-confidence of those who speak in this manner."

SPECIAL TOPIC: PHILISTINES

6:3 The wealthy leaders were "putting off" (BDB 622, KB 672, Piel PARTICIPLE; this
VERB appears only here in this form and only twice in the OT (cf. Isa. 66:5) the day of YHWH's visitation by

- divination (SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION)

- trying to ignore (cf. TEV) the covenant consequences of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29

The irony is that by their very acts they were hastening the day!

▣ "the seat of violence" This could refer to

- the leaders of Israel

- the coming invasion of Assyria

"Seat" (BDB 443) is understood as "throne," which is imagery for "reign."

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 6:4-7

4Those who recline on beds of ivory

And sprawl on their couches,

And eat lambs from the flock

And calves from the midst of the stall,

5Who improvise to the sound of the harp,

And like David have composed songs for themselves,

6Who drink wine from sacrificial bowls

While they anoint themselves with the finest of oils,

Yet they have not grieved over the ruin of Joseph.

7Therefore, they will now go into exile at the head of

the exiles,

And the sprawlers' banqueting will pass away.

6:4-6 This describes the elaborate drunken banquets of the self-indulgent rich of the northern tribes (i.e. Joseph in line 3 of v. 6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

6:4 "sprawl" The term (BDB 710, KB 769, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE) is used
again in Amos 6:7. It has a negative connotation. It is parallel to "recline" (BDB 1011, KB 1486, Qal
PARTICIPLE), which may have been an unusual way to eat at this time in Palestine. If so, then
both denote new, foreign, and non-traditional actions (i.e. pagan influence on Israeli leaders).

6:5 "Who improvise" The VERB "improvise" (BDB 827, KB 967, Qal
PARTICIPLE) is uncertain in meaning. It appears only here in the OT. In later Hebrew
it means "break off" or "divide" (e.g. fruit that drops off the tree or bush). The translation "compose"
or "improvise" comes from the Arabic root.

JPSOA suggests "they hum snatches of song."

It is just possible in this context that these revelers are desecrating

- David's melodies, poems used in temple worship

- the instruments used in the temple (LXX)

▣ "like David have composed songs" This is a historical allusion to David's musical background.

- David himself

- played for Saul, 1 Sam. 16:16,23; 18:10; 19:9

- appointed Levitical singers, 1 Chr. 6:31; 15:1-16:43; 25:1-31; 2 Chr. 29:25-30

- designed or used musical instruments in his songs, Neh. 12:36; 1 Chr. 23:5

- examples of David's music

- 2 Samuel 22

- most of first two books of Psalm (cf. Ps. 72:72)

(1) MT asserts 73 psalms

(2) LXX asserts 84 psalms

(3) Vulgate asserts 53 psalms

- called "the sweet psalmist of Israel" (cf. 2 Sam. 23:1)

"have composed songs for themselves"

instruments"

means "to think" or "to account," but BDB #1,5 suggest "invent" (NKJV, NJB, REB) in this context.

6:6

NASB

NKJV, NRSV

TEV, NJB, REB

This is not so much an expression of the sacrilegious use (cf. Dan. 5:2) of sacred
utensils (cf. Exod. 24:6-8; Num. 7:13) as it is an expression of their drunkenness ("bowls, not cups"; TEV, NJB, REB,
"you drink wine by the bowlful"). Some see this as a magical practice based on Isa. 65:11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "they anoint themselves with the finest of oils" Putting oil on one's face and arms was a sign of
gladness. Their actions are in contrast to the next line of poetry. They should have been grieving over the ruin of
their nation.

The VERB has a wide semantical field but is not used elsewhere in the OT for
festival anointing. In this context, it may take on another example of inappropriate use of a ceremonial practice
(i.e. covenant violation).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

▣ "the ruin of Joseph" Joseph married an Egyptian. They had two children who were adopted
by Jacob (Israel, cf. Gen. 48:8-22). Although the Messianic line came through Judah, Joseph received the "double
inheritance" of the oldest child. Joseph's two sons became the two largest tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh. They
were part of the ten northern tribes who broke away from Solomon's son, Rehoboam, in 922 B.C. and
started a new state under Jeroboam I. This new state was known by several titles:

- Israel (Jacob's new name)

- Samaria (capital)

- Ephraim (largest tribe)

6:7 This refers to YHWH's judgment on these who cared only for themselves, but claimed to know
God (i.e. the northern kingdom)! Their judgment is the exact reversal of their lifestyles! First in extravagance
and revelry; first in exile!

▣ "banqueting" This term (BDB 931, KB 634) is found only twice in the OT (here and Jer. 16:5). The
Jeremiah text (and one Ugaritic text) links this term with a self-indulgent pagan feast for the dead! If so, the sarcasm of
Amos' statement is obvious.

It is another example of Israel abusing YHWH's law by adopting pagan rites or flaunting Mosaic regulations.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 6:8-11

8The Lord God has sworn by Himself, the Lord God of hosts

has declared:

"I loathe the arrogance of Jacob,

And detest his citadels;

Therefore I will deliver up the city and all it contains."

9And it will be, if ten men are left in one house, they will die.

10Then one's uncle, or his undertaker, will lift him up to carry out his bones from the house, and he will say
to the one who is in the innermost part of the house, "Is anyone else with you?" And that one will say, "No one." Then he will answer,
"Keep quiet. For the name of the Lord is not to be mentioned." 11For behold, the Lord
is going to command that the great house be smashed to pieces and the small house to fragments.

6:8-11 The UBS, Handbook for Translators, p. 131, makes a good point that these verses parallel
Amos 5:21-24. With God's wrath (cf. Amos 6:8; 5:24) comes God's devastating, complete judgment!

6:8 "The Lord God has sworn by Himself" For "the Lord God"
(i.e. Adon YHWH), see note at Amos 4:2.

The VERB "swear" (BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal PERFECT) is used
several times in Amos referring to YHWH swearing

- by His holiness, Amos 4:2

- by Himself, Amos 6:8

- by the pride of Jacob, Amos 8:7 (sarcasm, irony, or regret)

▣ "the Lord God of hosts" The repetition of these two names for
Israel's Deity makes this an emphasized pronouncement.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (Adon and Kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "I loathe the arrogance of Jacob" The VERB (BDB 1060 II, KB 1672, Piel
PARTICIPLE) is a rare (only here in the OT) but a powerful term of rejection (see all the versions). BDB
has "loathe," KB has "to make repulsive, desecrate." It is parallel to "hate" (BDB 971, KB 1338, cf. Amos 5:21).

The term "arrogance" (BDB 144) means "exaltation," "majesty," or "excellence." It is used in a
positive sense toward Israel in Ps. 47:4. In this context it refers to Amos 6:4-6. See sarcastic parallel in Amos 8:7. Israel's
inappropriate "pride" receives God's judgment (cf. Hosea 5:5; 7:10)!

6:9-10 This is prose, not poetry.

6:9 "ten men" This number was important to the Jews because it was the minimum number required for worship
(in Babylon during the exile ten men were required to start a synagogue) and other social events, possibly even military groups. Because
of the use of the number ten, this judgment verse may relate to Amos 5:3.

6:10 This verse seems to describe the siege of Samaria, the capital of Israel. There will be so many
people dead and the plague so rampant that bodies will be burned indiscriminately (cf. Amos 8:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CREMATION

▣ "one's uncle, or his undertaker" There are many questions about this phrase.

- Are there two people or one?

- What does the word (BDB 976) translated "undertaker" by the NASB, but literally means "he who burns," mean?

For question #1 the phrase refers to two different people who talk together in the rest of the verse
(i.e. so there is no survivor in the recesses of the house).

For question #2 there have been many theories:

- one who burns deceased bodies

- embalming or anointing the dead with spices

- one who burns incense on behalf of the dead

- one who burns a sacrifice on behalf of the dead

- a parallel term for a near relative. The first term would mean a near kin on the mother's side and
the second term a near kin on the father's side.

For me #1 or #5 seems best. But #4 could be linked to the banquet for the dead in Amos 6:6.

▣ "Keep quiet. For the name of the Lord is not to be mentioned" This is
a theological affirmation of who sent the invasion. The aftermath of judgment causes a holy reverence for YHWH,
missing so long in Israel.

The phrase "keep quiet" (BDB 245, a Hebrew INTERJECTION) is used
in contexts of YHWH's presence (cf. Hab. 2:20; Zeph. 1:7; Zech. 2:13) and judgment (cf. Amos 8:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH, D.

6:11 This is the concluding point of Amos 6:8-11. Judgment (by a foreign nation, i.e. Assyria) will fall
on great and small (i.e. all the population). No one will escape (cf. Amos 5:18-20).

▣ "to pieces. . .to fragments" The first term's (BDB 944, KB 1249) meaning is uncertain:

- used of rain droplets (Song of Songs 5:2)

- chopped food

- to shatter or grind

The second term (BDB 132, KB 149) means to break open (cf. Ps. 141:7), like a wall (cf. Isa. 22:9). The
VERB form implies a tearing into pieces (Piel). David Allan Hubbard, Joel and
Amos (Tyndale OT Commentaries), asserts that these two terms fit an earthquake better than an invasion. He
also lists the other places in Amos where he thinks the texts fit an earthquake (cf. Amos 1:1; 2:13; 8:8; 9:1-6), p.198.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: AMOS 6:12-14

12Do horses run on rocks?

Or does one plow them with oxen?

Yet you have turned justice into poison

And the fruit of righteousness into wormwood,

13You who rejoice in Lodebar,

And say, "Have we not by our own strength taken Karnaim

for ourselves?

14For behold, I am going to raise up a nation against you,

O house of Israel," declares the Lord God of hosts,

"And they will afflict you from the entrance of Hamath

To the brook of the Arabah."

6:12 These first two questions are somewhat difficult in Hebrew, but it is obvious they refer to unnatural
acts. All these rhetorical questions expect a "no" answer. It was also unnatural for God's people to turn justice into poison!

▣ "Do horses run on rocks" "Rocks" (BDB 700, KB 758) refers to large boulders or possibly to horses running
up cliffs or over crags. The answer is obviously "no."

▣ "does one plow them with oxen" It is possible to change the MT's vowels and dividing of consonants to read "plow the sea"
(cf. NRSV, TEV, NJB, NET, JPSOA footnote). This is accomplished by taking the PLURAL ending of "oxen" as a
separate word, "sea." This fits the context better. As v. 12a, it is meant to be an impossible act. All four questions expect a "no" answer!

The UBS Text Project, p. 289, gives "with oxen" a "B" rating (some doubt). It assumes that line 2 refers
to "plowing a rock with oxen."

▣ "justice. . .fruit of righteousness" See note at Amos 5:12.

6:13 "You who rejoice" This Hebrew phrase implies arrogance and pride over two military victories by Jeroboam II of the
trans-Jordan cities of Lodebar and Karnaim. Israel was proud and confident in her military, but YHWH will destroy Israel by a greater
military power (cf. Amos 6:14, the Assyrians)! The Assyrians will come from the same geographical direction as these two cities mentioned, "the north."

▣

NASB, TEV, JPSOA
"Lodebar"

NKJV, NRSV, NJB
"Lo Debar"

Rotherham, NRSV footnote, REB, Peshitta
"in a thing of nothing"

The MT apparently has the name of a city (BDB 520, cf. 2 Sam. 9:4,5;17:27) but the
UBS Text Project, p. 289, gives "for nothing" an "A" rating (almost certain).

However, in context, Lodebar seems to be parallel to the city of "Karnaim" (BDB 902).

- MT ‒ "in Lo-debar" ‒ ל לא דבר

- Peshitta ‒ ללא דבר

▣ "Have we not by our own strength taken Karnaim for ourselves" This is apparently another
city in the trans-jordan area. The term (BDB 902) means "a pair of horns," which would denote its power. These
cities were both recaptured by Jeroboam II (782-753 B.C., cf. 2 Kgs. 14:25).

The theological implication of the phrase is that Israel, by her own military power, captured these
two cities, which goes against the concept of holy war. It was YHWH's power and strength (e.g. Exod. 13:3,14,16)
that enabled His people to win in battle. This claim is another sign of Israel's arrogance and covenant ignorance.

6:14 "I am going to raise up a nation against you" This refers to Assyria (cf. Isa. 10:5).

Land (cf. Num. 34:7-8; Josh. 13:5; Jdg. 3:3; 1 Kgs. 8:65; 2 Kgs. 14:25). Judah would also be affected!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation.
You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of
the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why did God reject the sacrifices of the northern tribes?

- Why is God's creative act emphasized? (Amos 6:8-9)

- Why is Amos 5:25-26 so difficult to interpret?

- Is Amos condemning wealth and the sacrificial system or something else? What?
